text:
A two-time Kentucky Derby winner was refused the front door of a Louisville hotel in 1961 at a banquet being held in his honor. Jimmy Winkfield stood on the sidewalk at Fourth and Broadway in a pin-striped suit with his daughter beside him while men upstairs waited to applaud him.

He had ridden for the Tsar of Russia and walked two hundred and sixty racehorses eleven hundred miles across a war to save them.

Louisville gave him a doorway he was not allowed to use.

The old man came up Fourth Street in a pin-striped suit and a fedora, with his daughter on his arm, and stopped at the front door of the Brown Hotel.

It was May of 1961. Inside, on an upper floor, a banquet room was filling with the best turf writers in America, and the dinner was being given in his honor.

Sports Illustrated had paid to fly him in from France. It had been fifty-eight years since he had last seen Louisville.

He was told he could not come in that way.

The man who told him, by one account, was the hotel's own doorman. A Black man in a uniform, doing the job the hotel paid him to do, standing in the one spot where the rule had to be said out loud.

So the two of them waited on the sidewalk at Fourth and Broadway. A man near eighty years old and his grown daughter, who had been raised in France and had never been refused a door in her life.

Somebody eventually went and found the magazine's people, and there were arguments. The organizers came down, the hotel relented, and the guest of honor was allowed to walk into the building where a room full of men were waiting to applaud him.

When he came in, most of the room found something else to look at.

One man crossed the floor to him. Roscoe Goose was white, and he had won the 1913 Kentucky Derby on a horse called Donerail at ninety-one to one, which is still the longest price ever to win that race.

The rest let him stand there.

His name was Jimmy Winkfield.

He had won the Kentucky Derby in 1901. He won it again in 1902, and no Black rider has won it since.

He was born in Chilesburg, outside Lexington, the youngest of seventeen children on a sharecropper's place. Sources put the year at 1880 or 1882, and nobody has ever settled it.

His first professional ride was a catastrophe. On a horse named Jockey Joe at Hawthorne in Chicago in 1898, he broke fourth from the rail and cut hard across three horses on the inside, and all four went down.

The stewards suspended him for a year.

He was sixteen.

He came back in September of 1899 at the Harlem track outside Chicago and won. Then he won thirty-eight more times that season, and the May brothers signed him to a three-year contract.

Col. Phil Chinn, a fixture of the Bluegrass horse establishment, watched him come up and said Bub May never had to teach that boy anything. The kid had no particular style, Chinn said, he just sat up there like a piece of gold.

In 1900 he rode a colt called Thrive in his first Kentucky Derby and finished third. It was the first of four Derby rides, and no jockey since has bettered what he did across those four.

That same year he went to New York looking for mounts. White riders there had organized what they were calling an anti-colored union, and the Black jockeys he had grown up admiring were standing around the backstretch unable to get work.

He went back to Chicago, and at the Harlem track a white jockey ran him into the rail.

He got up with a badly bruised leg. The horse had cracked ribs.

That was the method, and there was nothing unusual about it. Charles Parmer set the whole thing down in his 1939 history of American racing.

A Black rider would get pocketed and shoved back through the field. Or bumped off his line, or run wide, or a man would come alongside, hook a boot under his stirrup and lift him out of the saddle at speed.

Or the man beside you swung his whip wide while appearing to urge his own horse, and opened your face.

From the grandstand it read as a rough trip, and a steward saw nothing but racing. An owner saw an expensive animal come back sore and quietly hired somebody else the following week.

The New York Times put it plainly on 29 July 1900. The public believed the old Black riders had lost their touch, the paper reported, and racing men knew better, because a quietly formed combination had shut them out.

Winkfield was twenty years old, riding into that, and he had two Kentucky Derbies in front of him.

He took the first one in 1901 on His Eminence and led the whole way. He won a hundred and sixty-one races that year.

The second one is the ride they should still be teaching.

On 3 May 1902 he went to the front on a chestnut colt named Alan-a-Dale, owned, bred and trained by Thomas Clay McDowell, a great-grandson of Henry Clay. The colt was unsound and everyone in the barn knew it.

Winkfield opened up six lengths. Then, in the stretch, the horse went lame underneath him.

A rider gets a few seconds to decide a thing like that. Pull him up and save the animal, or hold him together and try to steal the biggest race in America on a leg that is coming apart.

He held him together.

He drifted the closers out toward the deep, slow going in the middle of the track. He kept the colt balanced and moving, and Alan-a-Dale went under the wire by a nose.

The horse did not race again that year.

Winkfield was twenty or twenty-two, depending on which birth year you believe. He had won the Kentucky Derby twice running, something only Isaac Murphy had ever done, and nobody would match it again until Ron Turcotte on Riva Ridge and Secretariat seventy years later.

He was making a thousand dollars a race. He had started at eight dollars a month.

Then it ended, and it ended over a horse race that was not the Derby.

Winkfield had given his word to John E. Madden, one of the most powerful owners in American racing, that he would ride Madden's horse in the Futurity. He took another man's mount instead.

Breaking a verbal commitment was a real offence and white jockeys did it too. What happened next was not what happened to them.

Madden went to every prominent owner he could reach and told them not to put Winkfield up. The number is in the record: three hundred and ninety-one mounts in 1902, two hundred and twenty-three in 1903.

He rode the odds-on favorite Early in the 1903 Kentucky Derby, took a lead of a length and a half, and got caught in the stretch and beaten by three-quarters of a length. He called it the worst loss of his life.

There was also the Klan, which had started sending him threats.

At the end of 1903 he bought a steamer ticket. He was twenty-one years old, he had a Russian-Polish-English dictionary, and he did not speak a word of any of it.

Russia decided he was magnificent.

He won the Emperor's Purse and the Russian Oaks five times and the Warsaw Derby, and by the middle of it he was earning something like a hundred thousand dollars a year in rubles. He kept a suite in the best hotel in Moscow and he employed a white valet.

He came back across the Atlantic to visit in December of 1909, and the New York Sun noticed how he had travelled. The headline read that a gentleman from Kentucky had come second class so as not to vex the intolerant.

A man who kept a suite in Moscow and dined with counts had booked himself onto the cheap deck for the crossing home. He had worked out exactly what an American ship would tolerate from him and he had priced it in advance.

In Russia he rode for Armenian oil money and sat for photographs in the newspapers. In America he was a Black man who knew which deck to buy.

Then, in 1917, the aristocracy stopped existing.

Racing died with it. Winkfield followed the Moscow racing crowd nine hundred miles south to Odessa, on the Black Sea, where a Polish horseman named Frederick Jurjevich had built a refuge from the war.

It lasted two more years.

On the morning of 4 April 1919, Winkfield woke to the sound of artillery on the edge of the city.

He was thirty-seven, or thirty-nine. Years later he said what he had thought lying there listening to it, which was that this was no longer a fit place for a small colored man from Chilesburg, Kentucky, to be.

Jurjevich had a plan and the plan was insane. Get the whole racing colony out overland, west and north to Warsaw, roughly eleven hundred miles across a continent that had just finished tearing itself apart.

Men, women and children. And two hundred and sixty racehorses.

Winkfield was made his second in command. He said he was damned if he was going to leave the horses behind to be eaten.

They walked.

Out of Ukraine, over the Transylvanian Alps, through what is now Romania and Hungary. A column carrying the most valuable bloodstock left in Russia and the people who had bred it, moving at the pace of a horse that cannot be hurried.

There was no food to buy. Villagers along the route robbed them, and in some places they staged races in the road to raise money to keep going.

It took three months.

Winkfield brought that column into Warsaw having lost eight or ten horses out of two hundred and sixty.

He was a jockey. He had been handed the most valuable horses left in Europe, a column of families, and a war to walk them across.

He rebuilt in France. There was a wife, a chateau with private stables in Maisons-Laffitte outside Paris, a training operation, and by the time he stopped riding in 1930 he had somewhere over two thousand six hundred wins to his name.

In 1940 the Germans came.

They took the property. One account has him facing them down in his own stable yard holding a pitchfork.

He got out with his family and reached New York in 1941, close to sixty years old. What America had for him was a jackhammer on a Works Progress Administration crew, and after that a job with the Bostwick stable at Aiken, South Carolina, working horses for wages.

The man who had ridden for the Tsar spent the war years mucking out in South Carolina.

He went back to France in 1953, reopened his stables, and started a school to teach young riders. Then in 1961 a magazine offered to bring him home for the Derby, and he took it, and he brought Liliane.

Which is how a two-time Kentucky Derby winner came to be standing on the pavement at Fourth and Broadway in the state where he was born, in a good suit, being told which entrance was his.

Three days later he sat in a box at Churchill Downs and watched the race as a spectator.

He went back to Maisons-Laffitte. He told people he had thought about selling up and moving home to America for good.

He never came back.

He died in France in March of 1974, ninety-one or ninety-three years old. American racing took another thirty years to say his name properly.

On 9 August 2004 the National Museum of Racing put him in the Hall of Fame at Saratoga Springs. Someone had to walk up and accept the plaque for him, and the person who did it was Liliane Winkfield Casey.

The same daughter. The one who had stood beside him on the sidewalk in Louisville forty-three years earlier while men decided whether her father could use a door.

Behind him the gate emptied out fast. Jess Conley brought a horse home third in 1911, the last Black rider ever to finish in the money.

Henry King finished tenth in 1921. Nobody in the stands understood they had just watched the last one for a lifetime.

The next Black man to get a Derby mount was Marlon St. Julien, of Lafayette, Louisiana, who rode a colt called Curule to seventh place in the year 2000. Seventy-nine years had passed.

Four Black riders have made it into that gate since 1921.

Since Alan-a-Dale came home lame and first in 1902, none of them has won.

There is a race for him now. Every January at Aqueduct in Queens, on the Monday they set aside for Martin Luther King, they run six furlongs and call it the Jimmy Winkfield Stakes.

Six furlongs on a cold morning in New York, for a man who won nearly every race worth winning in Europe and could not get through the front door of a hotel in the state where he was born.

text:
Minneapolis restaurant that offered free meals to protest ICE raids announces closure
Owner Dylan Alverson says he 'exhausted every option' after trying to keep Minnesota establishment operational 

Modern Times Café, a Minneapolis restaurant that attempted to eliminate prices, has announced it will be closing for good by the end of the year.

"For the last six years, I’ve been trying to prove that Modern Times can continue to exist," owner Dylan Alverson wrote on social media Saturday. "I’ve exhausted every option without compromising the core fundamentals that make Modern Times what it is."

He added that he plans to spend the next two months celebrating the 16-year-old business and discussing ways for a business like his to continue.

"The only way for places like Modern Times to exist in the future is to actively challenge the reasons why it can no longer exist," Alverson wrote.

31 items in my cart at self-checkout in Moore, Oklahoma.

One $12 pack of batteries did not scan.
Loss prevention stopped me and walked me to a back office.

Him: "Sign this admission and we do not call the police."
Me: "What does the form say?"
Him: "It says you intended to steal the twelve-dollar batteries."
Me: "I missed one scan out of thirty-one items. I can pay for them right now."
Him: "Just sign the form."

Me: "I am happy to pay for the batteries, but I am not signing that."

Under 22 O.S. 1343, an Oklahoma merchant may detain a person in a reasonable manner for a reasonable length of time to investigate suspected shoplifting.
Signing a store confession or admission form is completely optional.
Under 21 O.S. 1701, Oklahoma defines larceny as taking personal property accomplished by fraud or stealth, "with intent to deprive another thereof."

Criminal intent is a required element of the crime.
Under 21 O.S. 1731, larceny of merchandise valued under $1,000 carries up to 30 days in county jail on a first conviction.
A missed barcode scan does not prove criminal intent.
A signed confession hands over the one element the missed scan alone never proved.
You can stay calm, offer to pay for the item and decline to sign.
P.S. Look up 21 O.S. 1701 and read the last six words.

text:
You already know the system loves control. 

And listen, I know you don’t ever want to use a hospital. But if you fall and break a hip or have a bone in your arm sticking out, you have no choice. If you have a heart attack in the grocery store, someone else can have 911 on the way, even without your knowledge.

With the I Do Not Consent Form™ in hand, so far, every single patient age 18+ has been protected from hospital protocols — but this article brings out another layer, one that is important to know as a behind-the-scenes look at the “teachable moment” to boost compliance, and what the Preop Nurses may say or think (without telling you).

You schedule surgery. You sign consents for the procedure, anesthesia, and known risks. You go under. 

And while you’re unconscious, some hospitals have protocols to jab you (or your child) with a vaccine — flu, COVID, or others — without your explicit, awake consent. Because your paperwork already allows for it 👀.

This isn’t conspiracy theory. It’s published medical practice.

The “Teachable Moment” They Don’t Tell You About

Hospitals and anesthesiologists openly discuss perioperative vaccination as a way to boost compliance. While you’re out cold for surgery, they administer the shot. Reasons given: convenience, higher uptake rates, and eliminating needle fear in kids.

•Kaiser Permanente in Santa Clara offers flu shots to children under anesthesia for procedures like eye surgery or dental work. 

•Children’s hospitals have implemented standardized processes, with dramatically increased vaccination rates. One program went from ~140 to over 2,000 flu shots per year:

•Massachusetts General Hospital developed protocols for COVID vaccines during the perioperative period. See HERE.

In official medical literature and publications, they openly call it a “teachable moment.”

You signed the admission papers. 

Now, you are unconscious. You cannot say no in real time. Pre-op discussions may mention it vaguely (or not at all), and standing orders or team protocols can make it routine.

A “Teachable Moment”

The exact phrase is mentioned in published articles.

•Title: 2022 article in the journal Anesthesiology: ”Influenza Vaccination in Perioperative Settings: A Teachable Moment”

•Authors: Suchitra Rao, Tyler Morrissey, et al. (including researchers from Children’s Hospital Colorado)

•Published: December 1, 2022 | DOI: 10.1097/ALN.0000000000004341

‘Chaos in communication’: How shared clinical decision making for vaccines adds confusion

ワクチンの共同臨床意思決定が招く混乱―米国の接種推奨方針の変更

米国では、従来の定期接種推奨から、医療者と患者が個別に接種を判断する共同臨床意思決定への変更が検討されている。

B型肝炎ワクチンなども対象となる可能性がある。

CIDRAPの報道では、小児科学会や家庭医学会の専門家が、ワクチンの有効性や安全性に関する新たな科学的根拠がないまま推奨区分を変更すれば、接種の必要性に疑問を抱く人が増え、混乱を招くと懸念を示した。

従来、この方式はHPVワクチンの一部の年齢層など、個人によって接種の利益が異なる場合に用いられてきた。

推奨区分の変更が保険適用に及ぼす影響は不明だという。

CIDRAP reports that proposed changes to US vaccine recommendations could expand shared clinical decision-making to routinely recommended vaccines, potentially including hepatitis B vaccination. An Apollo Astronaut Claimed UFOs Could Be Demonic — But What Does Science Say? 🛸🌌

A man who once walked on the Moon later shared an extraordinary belief about one of humanity's greatest mysteries.

Apollo 16 astronaut Charlie Duke, who explored the lunar surface in April 1972, has expressed the personal belief that UFO phenomena could have a spiritual or demonic explanation.

It's a remarkable perspective from someone who witnessed Earth from another world.

But there's an important distinction: Duke's interpretation reflects his religious beliefs, not a scientific discovery or evidence of extraterrestrial or supernatural beings.

Scientists continue to investigate unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP), the modern term for many UFO reports. While some sightings remain unexplained because of limited information, NASA has emphasized that there is no credible evidence establishing an extraterrestrial origin.

An unidentified object is exactly that — unidentified. It doesn't automatically mean aliens, secret spacecraft, or supernatural forces.

When even someone who has walked on the Moon offers such an unusual explanation, it raises a fascinating question: What do you think is really behind the UFO mystery? 👀

text:
Billy Ray Hamilton (also called Billie Ray Hamilton or “Country”) was the parolee.⁠

While serving a short sentence at Folsom State Prison, he met Clarence Ray Allen. Allen offered him about $25,000 to kill several witnesses from Allen’s earlier case (including Bryon Schletewitz). After Hamilton was paroled in late August 1980, Allen’s son Kenneth provided him with money, transportation, and weapons. On or around September 5, 1980, Hamilton and his girlfriend Connie Barbo went to Fran’s Market near Fresno. Using a sawed-off shotgun, Hamilton killed Bryon Schletewitz (the main intended target) plus two bystanders who worked there—Josephine Rocha (17) and Douglas White (18)—and wounded two others. Police later found Allen’s “hit list” of witnesses in Hamilton’s possession when he was arrested a few days later during an unrelated robbery attempt.⁠

Hamilton was convicted of the three murders (plus other charges) and sentenced to death in 1981. He spent more than 25 years on California’s death row. He was never executed; he died of cancer on October 22, 2007, at age 58, after being transferred to a medical facility at Corcoran State Prison.⁠

His girlfriend/accomplice Connie Barbo received a life sentence.

🛢️🇺🇸US Big Oil is selling old fields and running its refineries flat out.

2 moves today show both sides.

Chevron is cleaning out the Gulf.

The company is exploring the sale of mature US Gulf assets. 

It’s an early, multi-month process that two people familiar with it say could raise about $1bn.

The fields on offer:
🔹Petronius: producing since 2000, partnered with Talos Energy
🔹Tubular Bells: producing since 2014, now 100% Chevron after the Hess deal
🔹Llano: a 50% stake inherited from Hess Corporation, operated by Shell, producing since 2004

The money is going to growth. 

Chevron is targeting 300,000 boe/d from the US Gulf by the end of 2026, led by Anchor, its first ultra-high-pressure platform and Ballymore, which can produce up to 75,000 b/d.

The timing is deliberate, US crude recently hit a 6 month high, so buyers are paying up for US barrels.

ExxonMobil, meanwhile, is dealing with a different problem.

A 50,000 b/d catalytic reformer at Exxon’s 275,000 b/d Joliet refinery in Illinois has been offline since 20 October, with flaring reported. 

Exxon says it is “working to resolve an operational issue.”

A reformer makes high-octane gasoline blendstock. 

Joliet supplies the Chicago area and the wider Midwest.

This is the risk of running refineries this hard. 

US utilization stayed above 95% for 11 straight weeks into August and Gulf Coast plants were still at 96% in October, when maintenance usually starts.

Upstream, the majors are selling their oldest assets while prices are high. 
Downstream, the refineries have almost no slack left.

TEXAS SENATE RACE — THIS ELECTION IS ABOUT MORE THAN ONE CANDIDATE

Normally, I would argue that Americans should vote for the individual, not simply the political party.

Character matters. Integrity matters. Experience matters.

But I believe the 2026 midterms are among the most consequential elections of my lifetime.

The issues extend far beyond individual candidates. Border security, constitutional government, economic prosperity, national defense, public safety, and America’s direction for the next generation are all at stake.

Republicans and Democrats offer fundamentally different approaches to many of these questions. Those differences deserve serious examination.

Consider Texas.

The latest Fox News poll shows Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico tied at 49% each, even though more Texans in the survey prefer Republican control of the Senate.

That tells us something important: Americans do not always vote according to party affiliation, even when control of Congress is at stake.

We should examine candidates carefully, understand the policies they support, and recognize the consequences of our decisions.

This election is about more than personalities. It is about the direction of the United States of America.

November 3 is approaching. Every eligible American has an opportunity to make a decision that matters.

God Bless the USA!

text:
Day 41/120

This afternoon, I had the honour of engaging with the Rotary Club of #Pflugerville in Austin, Texas, as part of my 20th Edition of the *Ivory Belongs to Elephants / Walking for Giants* campaign. I was also honoured to meet Rotary #DistrictGovernor Jeff Coleman and, separately, Pflugerville Mayor Doug Weiss.

Having provisionally engaged with 13 Rotary clubs on my journey, I continue to advocate for stronger partnerships in wildlife conservation, environmental education, and community engagement.

Connecting Texas and Africa through conservation, I see valuable opportunities for sharing knowledge and experience. 

Texas’s approaches to private-land stewardship and habitat conservation offer important perspectives, while African models—including community conservancies, wildlife corridors, and community-based tourism—demonstrate how local communities can become essential partners in protecting wildlife.

An elephant is worth far more alive than dead. Protecting elephants means safeguarding biodiversity, preserving habitats, supporting local livelihoods, and promoting peaceful coexistence between people and wildlife.

I invite Rotary clubs across the United States to partner with African conservation organisations and local communities to protect wildlife, strengthen environmental education, and build a sustainable future for generations to come.

As I continue my **3,700-mile journey across 11 states over 120 days, I remain committed to turning every step and conversation into an opportunity for conservation. 

When I walk, I create awareness. When I don’t walk, I talk!”

#IvoryBelongsToElephants #WalkingForGiants #RotaryInternational #TexasConservation #AfricanConservation #ElephantConservation #HumanWildlifeCoexistence #CommunityBasedConservation #CaringForOurCommonHome

Offering money to get people to vote, is illegal. 

Under 52 U.S.C. § 10307(c), paying or offering to pay someone for registering to vote or voting in covered federal elections can carry a penalty of up to $10,000 in fines and five years in prison.

In the 2024 presidential election, Musk's America PAC offered $1 million prizes to selected people who signed a petition and were registered voters in battleground states. The Justice Department reportedly warned that the scheme could violate federal election law.

In Wisconsin's 2025 Supreme Court election, the Wisconsin Elections Commission later found probable cause that Musk violated the state's election bribery law.

text:
Prince Narathip Praphanphong once offered Rama V money in exchange for regulations favouring his business. The king refused.

During the reign of King Chulalongkorn, Rama V, Siam’s economy expanded considerably. This followed the opening of free trade under the Bowring Treaty, signed in 1855 during Rama IV’s reign, and efforts to attract more foreign investment—particularly in infrastructure supporting the country’s modernisation.

Large amounts of Western capital flowed into public utilities and modern transport projects, including railways and trams. 

Danish businessmen, led by Phraya Chonlayut Yothin (André du Plésis de Richelieu), a Danish official serving the Siamese court, joined British investors in developing the Bangkok–Paknam railway and early tram services.

This period also saw more members of the royal family enter business rather than pursue government careers, although almost all had previously served in government. 

One prominent royal entrepreneur was Prince Narathip Praphanphong (กรมพระนราธิปประพันธ์พงศ์).

A younger half-brother of Rama V, the prince had served as deputy minister of the Royal Treasury but left government service after being accused of embezzling royal funds. 

He subsequently invested in rice mills, land, forestry, trams and railways. 

Almost all these ventures lost money, bringing him close to bankruptcy and forcing him to sell assets to repay his debts.

One revealing episode occurred when his tram business was struggling against competition from hand-pulled rickshaws. 

The prince, who then held the lower title of Krom Muen Narathip Praphanphong, petitioned Rama V to prohibit rickshaws from operating along streets served by his trams. 

In return, he offered the king 600 baht in cash per day. Rama V rejected the proposal.

The prince described the episode in a letter to Prince Svasti Sobhana, Krom Phra Svastivatana Visishtha:
“As rickshaws multiplied until there were some 8,000 throughout the city, people enthusiastically took to using them. 

Revenue on both the French and Thai tram lines fell by almost half. 

There were no profits to distribute, although we were not yet making a loss… At the time, I was a director of the Thai tram company. 

The directors proposed petitioning Rama V, offering 600 baht in cash per day in exchange for banning rickshaws from travelling along streets served by the trams, allowing them only to cross… His Majesty did not grant permission.”

Another concern was the substantial annual concession fee paid by the Thai tram company, while its French counterpart was exempt. In the same letter, the prince wrote:

“The French trams pay no concession fee at all, whereas the Thai trams have paid 50,000 baht a year for fourteen years. This has reduced the dividend to less than eight per cent per share, until the tram company could no longer distribute profits and was hovering on the brink of making a loss.”

Eventually, the prince’s tram business suffered losses that made continued operation impossible. 

A foreign-owned tram company bought it in 1908, bringing the royal-run enterprise to an end.

By Thanakorn Karisuk.

Images: King Chulalongkorn, Prince Narathip Praphanphong and trams during Rama V’s reign. 

Sources: the National Archives of Thailand, Fine Arts Department; the book “Encyclopedia of Royally Granted Rice Fields along Khlong Maha Sawat during Rama IV’s Reign”; and Silpa Wattanatham.

text:
“Siam Rice”: The princess behind England’s first Thai restaurant and its signature dish, “Khao Phat Mi” ร้านอาหารไทยโดยเจ้านายสตรี ร้านแรกในอังกฤษ เมนูเด็ด “ข้าวผัดหมี่”

Today, more Thais live abroad than in the past. Moving overseas brings living expenses and the need to earn a livelihood, prompting many to open Thai restaurants.

But a Thai princess pioneered this business in England decades ago. Her restaurant was Siam Rice, founded by Princess Churairat Siriman (พระองค์เจ้าจุไรรัตนศิริมาน).

What led her into the restaurant trade?

Under the absolute monarchy, royal women holding the rank of Mom Chao or higher received an annual royal allowance, with the amount determined by their lineage and rank. 

The Privy Purse paid these allowances, while women holding positions at court received an additional stipend. 

Whether employed or not, royal women therefore had a regular income that appeared to offer financial security without having to earn a living.

However, maintaining the lifestyle expected of their status involved considerable expenses, and the allowance alone was often insufficient. 

The worldwide economic depression of the late 1920s and early 1930s added further pressure. 

After the 1932 revolution ended the absolute monarchy, the People’s Party cut the budget for royal allowances, affecting royal women throughout the family.

These political, economic and social changes forced them to adapt to a different world. Many began earning their own living through trade.

Weerayut Pisalee described the princess’s business ventures in his article, “‘Feudal Traders’: How Royalty Adapted to Earning a Living after the 1932 Revolution,” published in the August 2015 issue of Silpa Wattanatham.

She began by supplying food under monthly arrangements to Mater Dei School and Bangkok Christian College, where her children studied. 

During school holidays, when she took them to Hua Hin for nearly two months, she opened Bar Chit Lom, serving seafood and other dishes.

In 1954, she moved to England with her husband, Prince Chatramongkhon Sonakul, to look after their children studying there. 

She opened Siam Rice, meaning “Thai Rice Restaurant,” on Kensington High Street. 

According to the article, it was then the first and only Thai restaurant in London, England and continental Europe.

One of its bestsellers was khao phat mi (ข้าวผัดหมี่), a dish she devised when opening the restaurant. 

She took the ingredients and accompaniments used in mi krop, Thai crispy noodles, and stir-fried them with rice instead of noodles. Its sour, sweet and salty flavours appealed to both Thai and foreign customers.

The restaurant also became a meeting place for Thai royalty visiting England.

Princess Churairat Siriman can therefore be regarded as a pioneer of the Thai restaurant business in the West.

By Suphawี Raksa
Images: Princess Churairat Siriman, Wikimedia Commons; the former Siam Rice building, Silpa Wattanatham, August 2015.

text:
Just let it sit there and do its thing until it gets down to almost no liquid. If you are using ethanol or a lower percentage ISO, you will have water left over and it will make it look cloudy and take longer to evaporate, but it will do so eventually. At this point, I will use a dab tool or whatever other object (I use a glass stirrer, but I’m sure most people do not have this at home) and stir it around to move the liquid material to the top because the concentrate will tend to float on top of it and create bubbles of water or solvent and you need to pop all of these and make sure it’s thoroughly dries it. This will only take about 2 to 3 hours doing it this way, but to be sure that all of the solvent has been removed, I would recommend leaving it there for at least 12 hours if not longer.
Once this is done, you have your solvent and you can dab it, add it to a joint or bowl, cook with it (assume it’s around 75% purity by weight to estimate dosage) or make a vape cartridge. 
Since this is easy, I’ll explain the vape cartridge. Whenever you use an alcohol based solvent to extract, concentrate like this, it will not grab all of the terps so I buy them and add six drops per gram. The terps are extremely expensive at $45 per 2 mL and very strong so you don’t need more than six drops, but you can add more/less to flavor. You will also need some sort of thinning solution which is easy to find on Amazon. I would highly recommend staying away from PEG but that will be the one you will see most common on Amazon; you want to find a natural terpene flavorless thinner, and @TrueTerpenes offers this as well but it’s pricey (and 100% worth it.) 
I have a little glass thimble sized container that I use to mix both of the terpenes; I will use my magnetic stir/heater to heat it up to around 100° but you can accomplish this many different other ways. You just need it to be hot enough to get liquidy but you don’t want it to get hot enough to start burning terpenes and cannabinoids. Whenever it does get liquidy, that’s when you put the appropriate amount of each and the thinner depends on which one you get.
While it is still warm, take a glass syringe with a blunt tip (22 gauge is perfect) and draw 1 g into the syringe and then fill the cartridge up and try to do it as equally as possible so I will go around the cartridge with it because it’s still quite thick even though it’s hot and thinner than it will be in the cartridge when it’s cooled. The last and very important part is to take each filled cartridge and put it back inside of the little container it comes in and put it upside down for several hours or overnight.
You are now ready to smoke your own vape cartridge and not counting the terpene or any other items you might have purchased it will only cost you about five dollars total to make. You also know that it is chemical free and you get to make your own flavor so it’s really fun and it saves you a lot of money. You might need to adjust the consistency, but it’s better to have it thicker than too thin because that’s when it will run through and start dripping out. If it is too thick, you can use a hairdryer to keep it running smoothly by heating it so that the solvent can touch the wicks again instead of the air channel that it makes from being too thick. Document everything you do and how much you use of everything and then the next time you will know how to adjust. 
I cannot stress enough that even though you might only be using drinking or rubbing alcohol, it is extremely flammable as a gas and can cause health issues so you don’t want to be closed up in a room with this and you don’t want it to be anywhere near a flame. I have done it with the road closed and the window open and I’ve had no problems but of course this isn’t the best option and not what I would recommend. Also remember that neither of these are meant to be smoked so if you have any doubts as to if it’s completely evaporated or not leave it longer.
Enjoy 🥰

text:
WHY IS PUTIN THE MONSTER WHILE ZELENSKY AND NETANYAHU GET DIFFERENT TREATMENT?

Why is Vladimir Putin consistently portrayed as the face of evil, while Volodymyr Zelensky and Benjamin Netanyahu receive markedly different treatment from Western governments and political leaders?

This is not an argument that Putin should escape accountability. The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023 over the alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children. Those allegations are serious and deserve scrutiny. "ICC source" (https://t.co/cv1b41mm7a)

But consistency matters.

On November 21, 2024, the same court issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity connected to Gaza. The allegations include starvation as a method of warfare, murder, persecution and other inhumane acts. These are judicial allegations, not convictions, but they are not trivial accusations. "ICC source" (https://t.co/z2hpGUZKqK)

Look at the political response. In April 2024, the U.S. State Department defended its position that the ICC lacked jurisdiction over the Palestinian situation while acknowledging the court's work on Ukraine. The official response rejected the comparison by declaring there was no moral equivalency between Putin and the Israeli government. That statement illustrates the very question critics are asking: Are international legal standards universal, or do they depend on whose government is being investigated? "U.S. State Department transcript" (https://t.co/UXLxTXM6uf)

And what about Zelensky? Supporting Ukraine's right to defend itself against Russia's invasion does not mean every decision by its leadership should be beyond scrutiny. Allegations of corruption, government misconduct, restrictions on political activity and the conduct of wartime authorities deserve examination on their individual evidence. Supporting a country under attack should never require unquestioning loyalty to its president.

The distinction is fundamental: a nation is not its leader, and an ally is not automatically innocent.

Western governments have strategic interests. Russia is a geopolitical adversary; Ukraine is a partner receiving Western support; Israel is a longstanding U.S. ally. Those relationships help explain why their leaders are treated differently in diplomatic policy. Whether every difference in treatment is justified must be judged against the evidence, the law and the circumstances—not political loyalty.

The real issue is not whether Putin deserves criticism. He does. The issue is whether the same determination to investigate alleged crimes, demand accountability and protect civilians applies when the accused is an ally rather than an enemy.

If international law matters, it must matter in Moscow, Kyiv and Jerusalem alike.

Justice cannot be universal in speeches and selective in practice. If leaders are to be judged by their actions, the standard must not change with the flag they represent or the strategic value they offer Washington.

text:
This is historically tone-deaf and selectively ignores the actual record.

George Washington did not sign the Treaty of Paris. The American signatories were John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, and John Jay. Washington was the military commander whose army (and the French alliance) created the leverage for those terms; he later resigned his commission once the war was over. Attributing the treaty to him personally is just sloppy.

More importantly, the treaty was not some generic “deal that ends wars.” It came only after Congress and the American side repeatedly rejected British peace offers that stopped short of full independence. The 1776 Howe mission and the 1778 Carlisle Commission offered various forms of reconciliation, autonomy, and tax relief without recognizing independence—offers the Americans refused. They fought on until Britain was forced to concede the core war aim. That is the relevant parallel Romney is drawing.

The same logic applies to Churchill. He (and the War Cabinet he led) rejected 1940 peace feelers that would have left Germany dominant on the Continent and Britain a secondary power. The war ended with unconditional surrender, not a negotiated settlement that preserved the Nazi regime’s gains. Pointing to the final instrument of surrender as proof that “deals happen” erases the deliberate refusal of earlier, worse ones.

Wars do end with agreements. The historical question is whether the agreement secures the objectives for which the war was fought, or whether it abandons them under pressure. Davis’s post treats the existence of the Treaty of Paris as a rebuttal while ignoring the years of rejected compromises that made its favorable terms possible. That’s the cherry-picking.

CHINA
SUPPORT AND LIMITS

Confirmed Chinese diplomatic policy:

Opposition to US–Israeli attacks on Iran.

Support for Iranian sovereignty.

Advocacy of renewed negotiations.

Support for Gulf–Iran dialogue and collective regional security.

Explicit opposition to Iranian attacks on Gulf states and disruption of navigation.

China therefore supports Iran without publicly endorsing every Iranian action. 

Beijing needs Iranian oil and values Tehran as a strategic partner, but also requires functioning Gulf energy markets and relationships with Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar. 

Credible but not fully public intelligence reporting alleges:

Chinese provision of satellite imagery usable for Iranian targeting.

Chinese dual-use electronics, guidance components and engines reaching Iranian defence networks.

Continued Chinese assistance with oil sales and sanctions evasion.

Chinese-origin air-defence equipment reaching Iran.

US Treasury has identified a Beijing-based Iranian defence representative coordinating weapons and dual-use procurement. 

US intelligence assessments attribute satellite imagery and weapons-component support to Russia and China. 

The underlying intelligence has not been released publicly**. 

China’s available options:

Continue buying Iranian oil through intermediaries.

Expand yuan settlement and non-Western banking access.

Provide commercial satellite data and dual-use components.

Offer diplomatic protection and mediation.

Replace damaged civilian and energy infrastructure.

Avoid open combat assistance that could trigger US secondary action.

Beijing’s preferred outcome is an Iran strong enough to resist Washington but restrained enough not to close regional energy arteries permanently.

RUSSIA
SUPPORT AND LIMITS

Russia has intensified high-level engagement with Iran. 

Lavrov’s Tehran visit emphasised the comprehensive strategic partnership, defence cooperation and Russian mediation. 

Putin has separately offered to use Moscow’s relationship with Tehran to support negotiations with Washington. 

Credible reporting and US assessments allege:

Russian satellite and targeting intelligence assisting Iranian strikes.

Continuing missile and defence-technology cooperation.

Russian technical support for Iranian supersonic cruise-missile development.

Russian-linked financial networks assisting Iranian sanctions evasion.

US Treasury says the Russian-linked A7 shadow-banking network processed transactions supporting Iranian oil sales, weapons procurement, the IRGC and Iran-aligned organisations. 

This is an official US allegation supported by disclosed transaction findings, not a Russian admission. 

Russia’s available options:

Intelligence and satellite support below the threshold of overt belligerence.

Missile, air-defence and electronic-warfare technology.

Financial and payment infrastructure.

Diplomatic cover and mediation.

Caspian logistics and industrial cooperation.

Information operations amplifying Western political division.

Moscow wants to complicate US operations, preserve its Iranian partnership and demonstrate great-power relevance. 

It does not want uncontrolled attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure that destabilise Russia’s relationships with Saudi Arabia and other producers.
